key_insight: MaxIM treats an AI system’s evolving memory as a compact summary that should preserve useful information, not simply recent history. It frames memory updates as an information-theoretic reward-shaping problem under a fixed capacity limit.
problem_solved: AI systems must compress ever-growing interaction histories into bounded memory. Training those memory updates with standard reinforcement learning is difficult because task rewards arrive late and provide weak feedback about which information should have been retained.
method: Formulate incremental summarization as updating a capacity-constrained memory.
Use an information-theoretic objective to guide what the memory preserves.
Apply reward shaping to address the credit-assignment bottleneck caused by sparse, delayed task rewards.
impact: The framework could help practitioners train memory-limited agents to retain information that matters for downstream tasks. The supplied abstract is truncated, so specific implementation details and empirical gains cannot be assessed.
visual_elements: An expanding interaction timeline feeding into a fixed-size memory box.
A memory-update loop: previous summary + new interaction → updated summary.
A comparison of sparse end-of-task rewards with feedback from reward shaping.
A capacity gauge illustrating the trade-off between limited storage and retained useful information.
paper_title: MaxIM: Maximally Informative Incremental Summarization via Reinforcement Learning
paper_authors: Jihwan Jeong, Guy Tennenholtz, Yinlam Chow, Chih-Wei Hsu, Craig Boutilier
